questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between Linux and Ubuntu?
options: Ubuntu is the kernel and Linux is the desktop environment that runs on it
Linux is the kernel; Ubuntu is a distribution that bundles it with tools, a package manager and defaults
They are two names for exactly the same thing
Ubuntu is a shell, like Bash, that runs on top of Linux
questions.explanation: Linux is strictly the kernel. A distribution such as Ubuntu packages that kernel with GNU tools, the apt package manager and default configuration.

questions.question: You are using WSL and your project lives under /mnt/c/Users/asha/code. Builds feel slow. What is the usual fix?
options: Move the project into your Linux home directory (~), because file access across the Windows boundary is slower
questions.explanation: Files under /mnt/c live on the Windows file system, and accessing them from Linux is much slower than using the Linux file system in your home directory.

questions.question: Your prompt changes from `asha@devbox:~$` to a prompt ending in `#`. What does that tell you?
options: You are in a directory called #
You are now in a zsh shell instead of Bash
You are working as root, the administrator account
questions.explanation: By convention, $ marks a normal user and # marks root. Root can change or delete anything, so take extra care at a # prompt.

questions.question: Why might a command from this course behave differently in the default macOS Terminal?
options: macOS is Unix-like but not Linux; its core tools come from BSD and some flags differ
macOS Terminal cannot run Bash at all
macOS uses the apt package manager with different versions
macOS runs the Linux kernel but with a different file system
questions.explanation: macOS ships BSD versions of tools like sed and ls, so some options differ (for example sed -i). For genuine Linux, use a VM or a container.
